headline: Riyadh's logistics zone has tenants building factories, not just sheds
deck: The Special Integrated Logistics Zone was designed to move goods through Riyadh. DHL and Lenovo have taken it somewhere else.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia's first special logistics zone, next to King Khalid International Airport, covers more than 32 million square feet. Its tenant list has moved beyond distribution: DHL Supply Chain has committed a large warehouse investment and Lenovo has broken ground on manufacturing inside the zone.
content:
The Special Integrated Logistics Zone next to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is the template the Kingdom's logistics estate programme is built on, and its tenant list has started to say something its designers may not have planned for.

The zone, developed and operated by the Special Integrated Logistics Zone Company and known as Riyadh Integrated, covers more than 32 million square feet and was the first of its kind in Saudi Arabia when operations launched. It offers the standard instruments of a logistics free zone: customs treatment, tax arrangements, streamlined regulation and land adjacent to an airport.

The intended use of such a zone is transit. Goods arrive, are stored, consolidated, relabelled, repackaged and forwarded, and the value added is in the handling. That is a real business and it is what most of the world's airport logistics zones do.

What has happened in Riyadh is more interesting. DHL Supply Chain committed a substantial investment to a new warehouse facility in the zone, which is the expected pattern. Lenovo broke ground on a manufacturing facility inside it, which is not.

A factory in a logistics zone is a different proposition to a distribution centre. It implies that the operator has concluded the zone's advantages — customs treatment on imported components, proximity to air freight for high-value output, regulatory simplicity — are worth more than the advantages of a conventional industrial city with cheaper land and heavier utilities. For products with high value density and short shelf lives in market terms, that calculation can favour the airport.

It also blurs a distinction that Saudi industrial policy has generally kept clean. Industrial cities under MODON provide land, power and utilities for manufacturing. Logistics zones provide customs and connectivity for goods in motion. A manufacturer inside a logistics zone is consuming both propositions, and its presence suggests the zones are competing for tenants that the industrial estates might have expected.

The national programme those zones belong to is large. Saudi Arabia's National Transport and Logistics Strategy targets 59 logistics zones by 2030 across more than 100 million square metres of planned area, with sites distributed to give access to both the Red Sea and the Gulf coasts. The objective is for logistics to contribute 10 per cent of gross domestic product.

Delivering that means building estates, and estates are construction: earthworks, roads, drainage, power distribution, water, fibre and the buildings themselves. It also means filling them, which is the harder half. A logistics zone with no tenants is a serviced field, and the difference between the two is a leasing effort that runs for years after the ribbon is cut.

Ports and terminals, along with multimodal transport, are declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo, which opens in Riyadh on 8 September.
author: Mo Qureshi
scheduledReason: Written ahead of the 8 September expo. It reports the zone's published scale and previously announced tenant commitments, not anything from the event.
